'''Helge Stjernholm Kragh''' (born February 13, 1944) is a Danish [[historian of science]] who focuses on the development of 19th century  physics, chemistry, and astronomy.<ref name="Institute"/> 
His published work includes biographies of [[Paul Dirac]], [[Julius Thomsen]] and [[Ludvig Lorenz]], and ''The Oxford Handbook of the History of Modern Cosmology'' (2019) which he co-edited with [[Malcolm Longair]].<ref name="Institute"/>

==Biography==
Kragh studied physics and chemistry at the [[University of Copenhagen]], graduating with a degree in 1970. He earned his Ph.D. in [[physics]] in 1981 at the [[University of Roskilde]]. He received a second doctorate, in [[philosophy]], from the [[University of Aarhus]] in 2007.<ref name="APS">{{cite web |title=Abraham Pais Prize for History of Physics: Recipient Helge Kragh Niels Bohr Institute, University of Copenhagen |url=https://www.aps.org/units/fhp/awards/recipient.cfm?first_nm=Helge&last_nm=Kragh&year=2019 |website=APS Physics |access-date=16 January 2020}}</ref>

Kragh was an associate professor of history of science at [[Cornell University]] from 1987 to 1989, a professor at the [[University of Oslo]] from 1995 to 1997, and a professor at Aarhus University in Denmark from 1997 to 2015.<ref name="APS"/>

As of 2015 he retired, becoming emeritus professor at the [[Niels Bohr Institute]] at the [[University of Copenhagen]].<ref name="APS"/>
He is also a professor emeritus at the Centre for Science Studies of [[Aarhus University]].<ref name="emer">{{cite web |title=Academic staff |url=https://css.au.dk/en/academic-staff/ |website=Centre for Science Studies Department of Mathematics Aarhus University |access-date=16 January 2020}}</ref>

Kragh's areas of study are the [[history of physics]] from the mid-19th century onward, the [[history of astronomy]], the [[history of cosmology]] and the [[history of chemistry]].  He is known for his work on the history of the [[periodic system]], early [[Quantum mechanics|quantum atomic models]], speculative [[cosmology]] and the [[Aurora Borealis|northern lights]].<ref name="emer"/>

*2019, [[Roy G. Neville Prize]] for ''Julius Thomsen: A Life in Chemistry and Beyond'' (2016), [[Science History Institute]]<ref name="Institute">{{cite web|url= https://www.sciencehistory.org/roy-g-neville-prize|title= Roy G.
